items.title: Final exam for that 1966 American literature college exam
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
Several days ago I posted a reading list from 1968 for a college course on Twentieth Century [American] Southern Writers.  The course required reading 16 works from 9 authors.  The final exam begins by asking the source for eight excerpted extended quotations, followed by writing an essay comparing the approaches of three of these authors on the subject of love relationships, followed by a second essay comparing/contrasting three of these authors with regard to the style and tone of "southern writers."  The final embedded page has some notes I scribbled down while trying to organize my thoughts.

The exam booklets were not returned to us, so I have no record (or memory) of what my answers were.  My transcript shows a B- for the course, which was quite satisfactory for my pre-med needs.  I wonder how I would do today were I to re-read the same books and re-take the exam (an interesting thought experiment which I don't plan to implement).  (But I may still re-read some of the books, many of which have left vague pleasant memories in my head).

items.title: "Feather letters" (Fjäderbrev) were forerunners of express mail
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
In the era before the invention of adhesive postage stamps, postal services in Scandinavia used feathers affixed to the envelope to indicate that delivery was urgent and should be expedited.  The envelope above has a wavy line (known as a meander) with two horizontal lines through it and several stylized "crowns" in the spaces (together known as a Crown Coil or Kronoslinga) indicating that this was to be sent through the Royal Swedish Crown Post
Extra feathers indicated increasing degrees of urgency.  The envelope above has both white and black feathers affixed, apparently indicating the need for transport both by day and by night.

items.title: When your home is on a wooded lot...
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
... sometimes the woods come to visit.
Several days ago we were startled by what sounded like rolling thunder on a storm-free evening.  A quick peek out back revealed the cause.  We knew the tree was dead, and has been so for many years, but we like to leave standing deadwood for the benefit of the insectivorous birds.  We have seen four different types of woodpeckers from that deck (Downy, Red-bellied, Red-headed, and Hairy) plus some 40+ other species of birds over the years.  Those recurrent joys fully justify the occasional hassle of cleanup duties in the yard, woods, and now the deck.  
We've been less happy with visits from local raccoons.  Having trees near the house is not a significant risk factor for raccoon molestations, because those critters are fully capable of scaling a brick wall at the corner.  Once on the roof they look for accessible soffits, and with those dextrous paws they can rip the soffits off in order to gain entrance into crawl spaces and attics.  We used Havahart traps for a while, but eventually contracted with a company called Skedaddle that sent out a crew of five young women with ladders, tools, and wire mesh to render the soffits raccoon-proof.
Now I have to find a neighborhood kid with a chain saw...

items.title: The night sky over rural New Zealand
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
To create his spectacular image – now viewed millions of times online – Brendan Larsen spent two hours in September snapping hundreds of photographs of the night sky over Mount Taranaki in the North Island.
Larsen, 51, says he set his camera up to take an unlimited number of eight-second-long shots, with a two-second gap in between each photo. “I left her running for two hours and captured 578 photos … That was the easy part.”
The hard part came next. Larsen spent about 45 hours layering the individual photos – each of which contained about 25 satellites – over one another, using Adobe Photoshop. Much of the time was spent painstakingly erasing stars, to reveal the satellites...

items.title: A college reading list from 1966
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
Nicholas Dames has taught Literature Humanities, Columbia University’s required great-books course, since 1998. He loves the job, but it has changed. Over the past decade, students have become overwhelmed by the reading. College kids have never read everything they’re assigned, of course, but this feels different. Dames’s students now seem bewildered by the thought of finishing multiple books a semester. His colleagues have noticed the same problem. Many students no longer arrive at college—even at highly selective, elite colleges—prepared to read books.
This development puzzled Dames until one day during the fall 2022 semester, when a first-year student came to his office hours to share how challenging she had found the early assignments. Lit Hum often requires students to read a book, sometimes a very long and dense one, in just a week or two. But the student told Dames that, at her public high school, she had never been required to read an entire book. She had been assigned excerpts, poetry, and news articles, but not a single book cover to cover...
Twenty years ago, Dames’s classes had no problem engaging in sophisticated discussions of one week and the next. Now his students tell him up front that the reading load feels impossible. It’s not just the frenetic pace; they struggle to attend to small details while keeping track of the overall plot...
In 1976, about 40 percent of high-school seniors said they had read at least six books for fun in the previous year, compared with 11.5 percent who hadn’t read any. By 2022, those percentages had flipped...
Carol Jago, a literacy expert who crisscrosses the country helping teachers design curricula, says that educators tell her they’ve stopped teaching the novels they’ve long revered, such as and . The pandemic, which scrambled syllabi and moved coursework online, accelerated the shift away from teaching complete works... At the prep school that I graduated from five years ago, I took a Jane Austen course my senior year. I read only a single Austen novel...
Some experts I spoke with attributed the decline of book reading to a shift in values rather than in skill sets. Students can still read books, they argue—they’re just choosing not to.Students today are far more concerned about their job prospects than they were in the past. Every year, they tell Howley that, despite enjoying what they learned in Lit Hum, they plan to instead get a degree in something more useful for their career...
For years, Dames has asked his first-years [university] about their favorite book. In the past, they cited books such as and . Now, he says, almost half of them cite young-adult books. Rick Riordan’s Percy Jackson series seems to be a particular favorite...

items.title: "Audio, video, disco"
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
The unofficial "motto" of TYWKIWDBI is "you learn something every day."  The phrase is not incorporated into the template title page, but I use it often as a closing statement when posting interesting stuff that's new to me.  

Earlier this week I encountered somewhere on Facebook the observation that the phrase "I hear, I see, I learn" is properly translated into Latin as "Audio, video, disco."  

I'm 60+ years away from my last Latin class, but I suspect there are some scholarly readers out there who can confirm or clarify this quite interesting discovery.

items.title: How to win at Monopoly
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
With a second monopoly completed, your next task is to improve those properties to three houses each, then all of your properties to four houses each. Six properties with three houses will give you more than half of the houses in the game, and four houses each will give you 75% of the total supply. This will make it nearly impossible for your opponents to improve their own property in a meaningful way. Keep the rulebook nearby once the supply gets low, as you will undoubtedly be questioned on it. At this point, you will be asked repeatedly to build some friggin’ hotels already so that other people can build houses. Don’t.
At this point, you more or less have the game sewn up. If losing a normal game of monopoly is frustrating, losing to this strategy is excruciating, as a losing opponent essentially has no path to victory, even with lucky rolls. Your goal is to play conservatively, lock up more resources, and let the other players lose by attrition.
Most board games are intrinsically competitive, but Monopoly does tend to bring out some of the baser instincts, and as Jason notes, it can also provide uncomfortable reminders of income inequality and business malfeasance in the real world.

items.title: Silver Linings Playbook (2013)
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
I first saw Silver Linings Playbook when it was released back in 2013, but I seem not to have blogged it at the time.  I'm doing so now for two reasons, one of which is to save and share the "Girl from the North Country" song by Bob Dylan, which was featured in the movie (some listeners will recognize the second voice in the harmony as that of Johnny Cash).  The subtitles are intermittently inaccurate; for lyrics see the link).
But I'd also like to recommend the movie, which to be honest is not easy to enjoy at first.  Even on a rewatch knowing how much I enjoyed it the first time, it was still difficult for me to tolerate either of the main characters for the first half hour or so of the movie.  Bradley Cooper and Jennifer Lawrence portray characters whose behavior varies from annoying to repellant, but by the end of the movie one finds oneself cheering for their success in overcoming their anxieties and obsessions.
For those curious about the movie I'll also embed the standard trailer below; the image quality is poor, but it offers a better presentation of the storyline than the musical version at the top.
